rationale: The review separates psychotic symptoms by dementia diagnosis and discusses formed visual experiences, other hallucinations and delusions. The Parkinson and DLB sections describe published clinical and imaging cohorts and cholinergic and serotonergic hypotheses. Its cited comparisons include perceptual tasks and presence or absence of symptoms. The review supplies no additional participant sample or dietary contrast.

The review distinguishes impaired reading, spatial localization and perception from other symptoms in posterior cortical atrophy. It discusses possible Lewy body pathology and cites separate case literature on abnormal visual phenomena. The review does not estimate visual event rates under an assigned exposure.

An aging-study participant developed formed visual hallucinations before observed parkinsonism. Dream enactment and fluctuating cognition were recorded separately, and visual experiences recurred later in the Lewy body dementia course. Medication changes and disease progression occurred during follow-up. The illustrative history gives no dietary comparison or count of episodes over a common window.

The paper examines laforin, abnormal glycogen and their links to Lafora progressive myoclonus epilepsy. Visual seizure phenomena concern that epilepsy syndrome. The studies reviewed do not supply a culinary fig contrast or a measured Parkinson visual symptom.

The Italian analysis includes 141 familial index cases. Cognitive impairment was more common among the C9ORF72 expansion cases than among participants with other ALS-related mutations (46.7% and 9.1%). Three index cases with associated behavioral-variant frontotemporal dementia had prominent hallucinations and delusions. The case material concerns an ALS/FTD phenotype and gives no uniform visual episode count or Parkinson food comparison.

The sections address dopamine biosynthesis and oxidation, tyrosine hydroxylase regulation, and therapeutic or experimental strategies. Visual hallucinations are discussed as clinical context. The work provides no independent visual episode endpoint linked to dietary intake.

The comparison included 17 people with DLB and 19 controls, with perfusion available for 15 and 19. Caregivers provided a past-month visual hallucination rating combining frequency and severity. In DLB the combined score correlated inversely with V4 perfusion (rho −0.52, p = 0.04). The visual-task BOLD responses did not show a significant association with that score. The contrast concerns imaging and a composite rating without an assigned food exposure.

The sample included 106 patients from 98 families across several dementia diagnoses, including four DLB and three Parkinson dementia cases. Descriptions of variant carriers include hallucinations amid broader cognitive and behavioral courses. The comparisons concern gene variants and diagnostic phenotypes. The report supplies no repeated visual event measurement tied to fig ingestion.

The article describes PET, SPECT and fMRI applications to dopaminergic and other systems, diagnosis, longitudinal progression and treatment assessment. Reported metabolic networks and reference citations for visual hallucinations are distinct from a primary episode-frequency comparison. It does not study dried figs.

One patient initially diagnosed clinically with Parkinson dementia experienced visual hallucination during a rapidly worsening course that included fluctuating consciousness and myoclonus. The paper places the clinical description in an atypical tauopathy series and includes a separate screen of pathologically confirmed idiopathic Parkinson cases. Neither the individual course nor the genetic screen estimates visual recurrence under a culinary exposure.

The review compares dominant, recessive and other genetic forms of Parkinson disease or parkinsonism. Visual and psychiatric features in particular SNCA or juvenile parkinsonism families are clinical descriptions. It does not distinguish a food exposure or provide new person-time counts of visual hallucination.

The 140-person phase II trial randomized participants with probable DLB to placebo or three donepezil doses. Table 2 combined hallucinations with cognitive fluctuation in NPI-2. Baseline table 1 counted participants with visual hallucinations separately from other modalities. Figure 3 compared changes in the broader hallucination item. These are different measures. No arm varied dried fig exposure.

The chapter reviews how Pittsburgh Compound B PET measures fibrillar amyloid-beta and compares patterns across dementias. The DLB section discusses phenotype and tracer findings. Its imaging and diagnostic comparisons supply no food-linked clinical visual episode frequency.

Records and neuropathology compare carriers of EIF4G1 variants. Selected case courses describe later delusions and hallucinations after motor or cognitive changes. Some narratives combine perceived presence, speech and visual material. They do not provide matched episode windows, an ingredient contrast or an estimate that separates the symptom modalities.

The recorded course includes visual hallucinations, cognitive decline and motor decline. The postmortem investigation established a different disease context, isolated central nervous system Whipple disease. The symptom narrative gives neither an episode rate nor a comparison with dried figs, and it cannot be treated as idiopathic Parkinson evidence.

The review considers orthostatic blood pressure, diagnosis, causes and interventions across autonomic disorders. It lists clinical features relevant to differential diagnosis. A visual symptom listing is distinct from a measured visual experience endpoint or a comparison of ingredients.

The study reanalyzes recordings from 13 Parkinson patients with dementia and 13 without dementia. Atlas-based beamforming estimates resting power and connectivity, with slowing and reduced connectivity in the dementia group. Visual hallucinations are mentioned in clinical background, with no separate group endpoint for their frequency. The analysis uses previously described participants.
